|---|---|

## A. Confidentiality Is an Independent Threshold Element

The attorney-client privilege codified at O.C.G.A. § 24-5-501(a)(2) does not attach to every exchange between a lawyer and a client. A communication is protected only if it was made, and maintained, in confidence. Confidentiality is not a gloss on the privilege, nor is it merely the flip side of waiver analysis; it is a discrete element that the party invoking the privilege must affirmatively establish. Its absence defeats the claim even where every other element — a genuine attorney-client relationship, a communication made to the lawyer in his professional capacity, and a purpose of obtaining legal advice — is fully satisfied. Because Georgia construes the privilege narrowly and assigns the burden of proof to its proponent, the confidentiality inquiry is frequently dispositive.

**1. The statute creates the privilege but does not define it.**

O.C.G.A. § 24-5-501(a) provides that certain admissions and communications are excluded from evidence on grounds of public policy, and subsection (a)(2) identifies communications between attorney and client among them. The statute does not enumerate the privilege's elements, allocate the burden of proof, or use the word "confidential" in connection with attorney-client communications. Those requirements are supplied by decisional law, and they were carried forward intact when the current Evidence Code took effect on January 1, 2013. The Editor's notes to § 24-5-501 expressly incorporate decisions rendered under former Code 1933 §§ 38-418, 38-419, and 38-1605, and under former O.C.G.A. §§ 24-9-21, 24-9-24, 24-9-25, and 24-9-27, in light of the similarity of the statutory provisions. The pre-2013 authorities discussed below therefore remain controlling.

A related but distinct source of obligation should not be confused with the evidentiary privilege. O.C.G.A. § 15-19-4 imposes on every attorney a duty to preserve the confidences of the client, and Georgia Rule of Professional Conduct 1.6 imposes a parallel ethical duty. Both are broader than the privilege: they reach information regardless of source and without regard to whether it was communicated confidentially. A party's showing that material is ethically confidential is therefore not a showing that it is privileged.

**2. The Supreme Court of Georgia treats confidentiality as a separate element.**

In *St. Simons Waterfront, LLC v. Hunter, Maclean, Exley & Dunn, P.C.*, 293 Ga. 419, 746 S.E.2d 98 (2013), the Court identified the conditions under which a law firm may assert the privilege over communications with its own in-house counsel: (i) a genuine attorney-client relationship between the firm's lawyers and in-house counsel; (ii) communications intended to advance the firm's interest in limiting exposure to liability rather than the client's interest in obtaining sound legal representation; (iii) communications conducted and maintained in confidence; and (iv) no applicable exception. Condition (iii) is stated as a freestanding requirement, coordinate with — not derivative of — the existence of the relationship and the purpose of the communication.

Although *St. Simons* arose in the law-firm setting, its framework is not confined there. The Court granted certiorari to address that specific context but held that the same basic analysis conducted to assess privilege in every other variation of the attorney-client relationship applies equally to it. *Id.* at 419. Condition (iii) is thus a general requirement of Georgia privilege law, and *St. Simons* is the cleanest available authority for the proposition that confidentiality must be independently established.

**3. The purpose of the privilege confirms that confidentiality is a condition of protection, not a consequence of it.**

The privilege exists for the protection and benefit of the client rather than the attorney; it is designed to secure the client's confidence in the secrecy of his communications and to promote greater freedom of consultation between clients and their legal advisers. *Marriott Corp. v. American Academy of Psychotherapists, Inc.*, 157 Ga. App. 497, 277 S.E.2d 785 (1981). The Supreme Court has more recently described it as the oldest of the privileges for confidential communications known to the common law, and long recognized in Georgia. *State v. Ledbetter*, 318 Ga. 457, 461-62 (2024). Its object is to encourage full and frank communication between attorneys and their clients and thereby to promote broader public interests in the observance of law and the administration of justice. *St. Simons Waterfront*, 293 Ga. at 421-22 (quoting *Upjohn Co. v. United States*, 449 U.S. 383, 389 (1981)); *accord Hill, Kertscher & Wharton, LLP v. Moody*, 308 Ga. 74, 78-79, 839 S.E.2d 535 (2020).

That rationale supplies the analytical reason confidentiality operates as a threshold condition. The privilege is justified by the need to protect an expectation of secrecy. Where the client held no such expectation, the communication presents nothing the privilege was designed to protect, and extending the privilege would exclude probative evidence without advancing any interest the rule was created to serve.

**4. Narrow construction and the allocation of the burden operate against the proponent.**

A narrow construction of the privilege, inasmuch as its exercise results in the exclusion of evidence, comports with the view that the ascertainment of as many facts as possible leads to the truth — the object of all legal investigation. *Tenet Healthcare Corp. v. Louisiana Forum Corp.*, 273 Ga. 206, 208, 538 S.E.2d 441 (2000). Courts are accordingly directed to confine the privilege to the narrowest permissible limits of the statute creating it, in order to permit liberal discovery. *Atlantic Coast Line R.R. v. Daugherty*, 111 Ga. App. 144, 141 S.E.2d 112 (1965).

Consistent with that construction, the burden rests on the party asserting the privilege to establish its applicability. *Zielinski v. Clorox Co.*, 270 Ga. 38, 40(2), 504 S.E.2d 683 (1998); *McKesson HBOC, Inc. v. Adler*, 254 Ga. App. 500, 562 S.E.2d 809 (2002). Where the client is an entity, the burden is on the corporation to establish that the advice at issue was privileged legal advice and thus not subject to discovery. *Southern Guar. Ins. Co. v. Ash*, 192 Ga. App. 24, 27, 383 S.E.2d 579 (1989). The practical consequence is that a silent or ambiguous record on the circumstances of a communication — who was present, who received it, and what the client expected — is resolved against the party claiming protection.

These principles govern the *scope* of the privilege, not its *strength*. Once a matter is properly found to fall within the privilege, it is absolute and is not discoverable. *Daugherty*, 111 Ga. App. at 149. Waiver, correspondingly, occurs only in very limited circumstances, *Alston & Bird LLP v. Mellon Ventures II, L.P.*, 307 Ga. App. 640, 706 S.E.2d 652 (2010), and inadvertent disclosure of a privileged communication does not effect one, *Lazar v. Mauney*, 192 F.R.D. 324 (N.D. Ga. 2000). The contested ground in most Georgia disputes is therefore whether the privilege attached at all.

**5. Confidentiality is measured by the client's intended audience; a communication made for onward transmission is never privileged.**

Communications made by a client to an attorney for the purpose of being imparted by the attorney to others do not fall within the statute. *Fowler v. Sheridan*, 157 Ga. 271, 121 S.E. 308 (1924); *accord Riley v. State*, 180 Ga. 869, 181 S.E. 154 (1935). The privilege is likewise not implicated as to testimony concerning information a client instructs counsel to convey to third persons. *Shelton v. State*, 206 Ga. App. 579, 426 S.E.2d 69 (1992). And an attorney is not barred from testifying about matters that occurred in the presence of the opposing party, because such communications were not intended to be confidential. *Martinez v. Housing Auth.*, 264 Ga. App. 282, 590 S.E.2d 245 (2003).

This line of authority is analytically distinct from waiver, and the distinction should be preserved in argument. In *Fowler*, *Riley*, *Shelton*, and *Martinez*, the privilege never attached; there was no protection to relinquish. That distinction carries practical weight given the narrowness of Georgia waiver doctrine. A party may successfully resist a waiver argument — establishing that no voluntary and knowing relinquishment occurred, or that a disclosure was inadvertent — and nonetheless lose the communication because the requisite expectation of confidentiality was absent from the outset. Framing the issue as one of attachment rather than waiver relieves the opponent of the heavier showing that waiver doctrine demands.

**6. Confidentiality cannot be conferred on material that lacks it.**

Neither the identity of the recipient nor the involvement of counsel supplies the missing element. The privilege does not encompass matters of which the attorney has or gains knowledge through a source other than the client's communications, and where the attorney has such knowledge from another source, testimony concerning it is proper. *Buffington v. McClelland*, 130 Ga. App. 460, 203 S.E.2d 575 (1973). One cannot render privileged that which is otherwise not privileged merely by placing it in the hands of an attorney. *Daugherty*, 111 Ga. App. 144. Nor do pre-existing facts acquire protection by inclusion in a document routed to counsel: admissions as to the value of property were not the advice of a professional adviser and could not be considered part of a privileged consultation simply because that evidence was included in a loan application. *Clayton County Bd. of Tax Assessors v. Lake Spivey Golf Club, Inc.*, 207 Ga. App. 693, 428 S.E.2d 687 (1993). The mere fact of employment between attorney and client is similarly unprotected. *Cranford v. Cranford*, 120 Ga. Its absence defeats the claim even where the remaining elements are fully satisfied: a genuine attorney-client relationship, a communication made to the attorney in a professional capacity, and a purpose of obtaining legal advice. ### 1. The Statute Creates the Privilege but Does Not Define It.

O.C.G.A. § 24-5-501(a) provides that certain admissions and communications are excluded from evidence on grounds of public policy, and subsection (a)(2) identifies communications between attorney and client among them. The statute does not enumerate the privilege's elements, allocate the burden of proof, or use the word "confidential" in connection with attorney-client communications. Those requirements are supplied by decisional law, and they were carried forward intact when the current Evidence Code took effect on January 1, 2013. The Editor's notes to O.C.G.A. § 24-5-501 expressly incorporate decisions rendered under former Code 1933 §§ 38-418, 38-419, and 38-1605, and under former O.C.G.A. §§ 24-9-21, 24-9-24, 24-9-25, and 24-9-27, among others, in light of the similarity of the statutory provisions. The pre-2013 authorities discussed below therefore remain applicable.

A related but distinct source of obligation should not be confused with the evidentiary privilege. O.C.G.A. § 15-19-4 imposes on every attorney a duty to preserve the confidences of the client, and Georgia Rule of Professional Conduct 1.6 imposes a parallel ethical duty. Both are broader than the privilege: they reach information regardless of source and without regard to whether it was communicated confidentially. Establishing that material is ethically confidential therefore does not establish that it is privileged.

Condition (iii) is a requirement in its own right. Confidentiality does not follow automatically from the existence of the relationship or from the client's purpose in seeking advice; it must be established separately.

Although *St. Simons* arose in the law-firm setting, its framework is not confined there. The Supreme Court of Georgia granted *certiorari* to address that specific context, but held that the analysis governing every other variation of the attorney-client relationship governs the law-firm setting as well. *St. Simons Waterfront*, 293 Ga. at 419. Condition (iii) is therefore a general requirement of Georgia privilege law, and *St. Simons* is the clearest Georgia authority for the proposition that confidentiality must be established independently.

Courts are accordingly directed to confine the privilege to the narrowest permissible limits of the statute creating it, in order to permit liberal discovery. *Atlantic Coast Line R.R. v. Daugherty*, 111 Ga. App. 144, [pin] (1965).

Consistent with that construction, the burden rests on the party asserting the privilege to establish its applicability. *Zielinski v. Clorox Co.*, 270 Ga. 38, 40 (1998); *McKesson HBOC, Inc. v. Adler*, 254 Ga. App. 500, [pin] (2002). Where the client is an entity, the burden is on the corporation to establish that the advice at issue was privileged legal advice and thus not subject to discovery. *Southern Guar. Ins. Co. v. Ash*, 192 Ga. App. 24, 27 (1989). A silent or ambiguous record on the circumstances of a communication (who was present, who received it, and what the client expected) is therefore resolved against the party claiming protection.

These principles govern the scope of the privilege, not its strength. Once a matter is properly found to fall within the privilege, it is absolute and is not discoverable. *Daugherty*, 111 Ga. App. at 149. Waiver, correspondingly, occurs only in very limited circumstances, *Alston & Bird LLP v. Mellon Ventures II, L.P.*, 307 Ga. App. 640, [pin] (2010), and inadvertent disclosure of a privileged communication does not result in waiver, *Lazar v. Mauney*, 192 F.R.D. 324, [pin] (N.D. Ga. 2000) (applying Georgia law). The contested ground in most Georgia disputes is therefore whether the privilege attached in the first place.

### 5. The Inquiry Turns on the Client's Intended Audience at the Time of the Communication.

Confidentiality is assessed by reference to whom the client intended to reach. Communications made by a client to an attorney for the purpose of being imparted by the attorney to others do not fall within the statute. *Fowler v. Sheridan*, 157 Ga. 271, [pin] (1924); *accord Riley v. State*, 180 Ga. 869, [pin] (1935). The privilege is likewise not implicated as to testimony concerning information a client instructs counsel to convey to third persons. *Shelton v. State*, 206 Ga. App. 579, [pin] (1992). An attorney is also not barred from testifying about matters that occurred in the presence of the opposing party, because such communications were not intended to be confidential. *Martinez v. Housing Auth.*, 264 Ga. App. 282, [pin] (2003).

Two features of this authority merit emphasis. The inquiry is directed to the client's intent at the moment of the communication rather than to the sensitivity of its subject matter. A communication on the most sensitive subject imaginable is unprotected if the client meant it to be relayed onward, and a mundane one is protected if the client meant it to remain between attorney and client. The inquiry is also objective in application. Because the proponent bears the burden, an assertion of subjective expectation unsupported by the surrounding circumstances will not carry it.

These cases turn on attachment rather than waiver, and the distinction should be preserved in argument. In *Fowler*, *Riley*, *Shelton*, and *Martinez*, the privilege never attached; there was no protection to relinquish and therefore no occasion for waiver analysis. The distinction carries practical weight, because Georgia waiver doctrine is demanding. Waiver occurs only in very limited circumstances. *Alston & Bird*, 307 Ga. App. at [pin]. Production of privileged material in the course of discovery has been held not to result in waiver. *Marriott Corp.*, 157 Ga. App. at 502. A witness's invocation of the privilege has been upheld even where the information had been voluntarily disclosed at a previous trial. *Ga. Osteopathic Hosp., Inc. v. O'Neal*, 198 Ga. App. 770, 779 (1991). An opponent proceeding on a waiver theory therefore assumes a substantial burden. An opponent proceeding on an attachment theory carries no comparable burden; the burden of proof remains with the proponent throughout, and a gap in the proponent's showing resolves the question against it. Where the record permits either framing, the attachment framing is the stronger one.

### 6. Confidentiality Cannot Be Conferred on Material That Lacks It.

Involving an attorney does not supply the missing element, and neither does routing a document through one. The privilege does not encompass matters of which the attorney has or gains knowledge through a source other than the client's communications, and where the attorney has such knowledge from another source, testimony concerning it is proper. *Buffington v. McClelland*, 130 Ga. App. 460, [pin] (1973). One cannot render privileged that which is otherwise not privileged merely by placing it in the hands of an attorney. *Daugherty*, 111 Ga. App. at [pin]. The subsequent transmission of a statement to an attorney for use in preparing a defense to litigation arising out of the underlying occurrence does not convert that statement into a communication to the attorney or bring it within the privileged category. *Id.*

Pre-existing facts do not acquire protection by inclusion in a document sent to counsel. Admissions as to the value of property were not the advice of a professional adviser and could not be treated as part of a privileged consultation simply because that evidence appeared in a loan application. *Clayton County Bd. of Tax Assessors v. Lake Spivey Golf Club, Inc.*, 207 Ga. App. 693, [pin] (1993). The mere fact of employment between attorney and client is likewise unprotected, *Cranford v. Cranford*, 120 Ga. App. 470, [pin] (1969), and evidence confined to that fact is not objectionable on the ground that it involves confidential relations, *Fowler*, 157 Ga. at [pin].

Where a single document contains both privileged and unprivileged material, the appropriate remedy is redaction rather than wholesale protection or wholesale production. Ample remedy exists to delete privileged matter, and this lies within the inherent power of the court. *Cranford*, 120 Ga. App. at [pin].

### 7. Where Confidentiality Is Established, the Protection Is Substantive and Broad.

The demanding character of the confidentiality requirement should not be mistaken for a narrow privilege. Once the element is satisfied, the protection Georgia affords is expansive in three respects.

The privilege is broad in its coverage. It is not confined to matters expressly communicated, but extends to items as to which the attorney acquired knowledge by his own observation where that observation was the result of professional employment. Nor is it limited to matters relating to litigation; it reaches all cases in which the attorney is consulted in the line of his profession. *Taylor v. Taylor*, 179 Ga. 691, [pin] (1934).

The exclusion the privilege works is substantive rather than procedural. The statute does not simply proscribe the channel through which evidence reaches the jury; it renders the evidence itself inadmissible. *Georgia Int'l Life Ins. Co. v. Boney*, 139 Ga. App. 575, [pin] (1976). An opponent therefore cannot cure the problem by locating an alternative witness through whom to introduce the same communication.

The privilege also applies without regard to how the material surfaced. It bars the communication whether it was voluntarily produced by the attorney to be used against the client or was surreptitiously or otherwise taken from the attorney's possession. *McKie v. State*, 165 Ga. 210, [pin] (1927).

The protection remains bounded by the content of the confidential communication. Documents may be admitted for limited non-communicative purposes, such as comparison of handwriting. *Guy v. State*, 138 Ga. App. 11, [pin] (1976).

### 8. Summary.

Confidentiality functions as a gatekeeping element. The proponent must establish it affirmatively; the governing narrow construction resolves doubt against protection; and the inquiry turns on the client's intended audience at the moment of the communication rather than on the sensitivity of the subject matter or the involvement of counsel. Where the element fails, the privilege never attached, and the opponent is relieved of the demanding showing that Georgia waiver doctrine requires. Where the element is satisfied, the resulting protection is absolute.

That framework governs the balance of this Part. The effect of a third person's participation in an attorney-client communication, addressed in Part I.B below, and the effect of circulation among an organization's own personnel, addressed in Parts I.C and I.D, are applications of the confidentiality element rather than exceptions to the privilege.
